en: *The Commentary on the Exposition of the Mind through Causes and Conditions: A Record of Resolution*, one fascicle.
In preparing to explain this treatise, I shall first analyze it by means of four sections, and thereafter explain the text of the main treatise itself.
Regarding these four sections: first, clarifying the author of the treatise; second, clarifying the [purpose of] composing the treatise... [text continues].
I. On whether the treatises expounded by the Three Vedas constitute valid authority. IV.
Discerning the fundamental tenets of the treatises.
The initial statement clarifies the author of this treatise:
namely, the Great Master Nāgārjuna, who had perfected his own and others' welfare, realized the Stage of Supreme Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi),
and clearly perceived the profound nature of dependent origination.
The *Sugatamatavibhaṅgabhāṣya*, whose fame is widely renowned and which was composed by one endowed with all virtues,
explains in its second section the reasons for composing this treatise.

This means that the Great Master Nāgārjuna, wishing to sever the net of doubts of his disciples endowed with the five virtues, and desiring to destroy the heterodox views of permanence and annihilation as well as all perverse attachments,
sought to cause future beings of dull faculties and those of sharp faculties alike to thoroughly understand dependent origination and clearly comprehend the two truths.

This treatise is composed for the purpose of swiftly attaining the true cause of unsurpassed bodhi. Now, those who wish to practice the true cause of unsurpassed bodhi must first thoroughly understand dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the nature of conditions (*pratyayatā*), clearly discerning the categories of affliction and purification, and having a lucid understanding of the principles of the two truths (*satyadvaya*).
Regarding the "two truths," these are the two kinds of truth: the ultimate (paramārtha) and the conventional (saṃvṛti).
Regarding the ultimate truth, it is the nature and characteristics of all phenomena, which are without arising or origination, neither annihilated nor eternal.
It transcends the path of language and ceases the sphere of mental activity;
it is a realm realized only by the noble ones through their own direct experience.
Regarding conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), briefly stated, there are four types.
First, the real;
second, the unreal;
third, that which approximates the ultimate truth.

Regarding the four purities, "reality" refers to the fact that although internal and external dependent origination is empty and devoid of substance from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*),
it nevertheless accomplishes manifest phenomena through the power of causes and conditions, like an illusion, by way of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).
The noble ones perceive its faults, whereas ordinary fools cling to it as real and do not see its peril;
they remain for a long time in the cycle of birth and death, attached to the phenomena of cause and effect produced through volitional activity. To say that these are not true means:
This refers to such things as mirages, illusions, and cities of the gandharvas;
within the framework of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), these do not establish any functional reality.
Even ordinary people understand that they are not truly existent without relying on the teachings of the Noble Ones. As for the term "approximating ultimate truth" (*neyārtha-paramārtha*):
In order to express the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya),
the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra),
and others have established and provisionally designated the twelvefold teaching by means of the sets of names, phrases, and syllables (nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya).

Although name, phrase, and syllable are not the primary reality (*vastu*), if names and so forth did not exist, one could not manifest phenomena; therefore, names, phrases, and so forth are called "proximate ultimate truth" (*upādāya-paramārtha*). As for the term "purified":

That is to say, all the vast merits of the Buddhas, Tathāgatas—such as the primary and secondary marks, the powers, and the fearlessnesses—are not produced by the unwholesome karma and defiled afflictions of ordinary beings.
It is called "pure" because it arises solely from the white, supramundane dharmas of the path.
Third, regarding the question of whether the treatise composed here constitutes a valid authority (*pramāṇa*),
there is an inquiry within this context.
The dependent origination and the nature of conditions taught by the Tathāgata are extremely profound and subtle;
although they can be understood, they are realized solely by the Buddha.
At what stage of attainment did the Great Master Nāgārjuna reside?
This treatise composed here is to be accepted as authoritative and trustworthy. Answer:
Because it is established through both scripture and reasoning, this treatise is free from error.
Take this as the authoritative standard and do not give rise to doubt. Regarding its establishment through scriptural authority (*āgama*),
the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
In the kingdom of South India, there was a monk of renowned virtue named Nāgārjuna,
who was able to refute the tenets of both existence and non-existence.

He shall manifest my unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma within the world, attain the first stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi), and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss (Sukhāvatī). Furthermore, the *Mahāmegha-sūtra* states:
"After my parinirvāṇa, there will be a bhikṣu named Nāgārjuna."
Able to destroy evil views and protect my True Dharma,
he appeared simultaneously with King Śubhakarmā;
possessing such authoritative teaching, he received this prediction.
Therefore, this master composed [this work] as something to be trusted, establishing it through reasoning.
This master, while in the world, realized the *śūnyatā-garbha-samādhi*;
by gesturing toward space, he brought forth jewels that fulfilled the wishes of sentient beings.
There is no obstruction even by mountain rocks or cliffs.
Furthermore, his other superior virtues are not described here for fear of excessive detail,
as they are clarified in other places.
Based on this direct perception, one may infer that this teacher is not an ordinary person.
His spoken teachings are the authoritative standard of the noble ones,
worthy of being transmitted and circulated.
Regarding the four statements that distinguish the tenets of our school:
while the Master was in the world, the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna were each without discrepancy;
they were mutually consistent with what the Buddha had taught, and [the disciples] practiced in accordance with those teachings.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the teachings of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna were interpreted by various masters with differing mental attachments,
each establishing numerous schools as described elsewhere.
Now, regarding this treatise:
The tenets to be expounded are not Small but Great;
within the Great Vehicle, they are further divided into three tenets.
The first is that all things are empty in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Second, the perfect reality that accords with principle;
third, the perfect interfusion of the dharma-nature.
This treatise is intended for those who, following the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, establish their tenets based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* and other such scriptures.
Therefore, this treatise is subsumed under the school that maintains the emptiness of all ultimate reality (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Regarding the subsequent statement explaining the main body of the text,
it is divided into two parts.
First, the explanation of the title;
second, the exposition of the main treatise.
Regarding the phrase "Verses on the Treatise on the Mind of Causes and Conditions" (*Hetupratyayacittavāda-kārikā*) within the explanation of the title:
Now, the names established in the various sūtras and śāstras all possess four meanings:
first, the person;
second, the location.
There are three metaphors and four meanings;
this present name is established based on these meanings.
For this reason, within this treatise,
all the meanings of dependent origination— both extensive and concise— as well as mundane and supramundane affliction and its cessation, spoken by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, [are presented].
Because all such meanings are fully subsumed herein, this name is established.
As for the term "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*), it excludes the various evil views such as those of nihilism, eternalism, and causelessness. As for the term "causes and conditions":
Why is this so? It is because the two treatises, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-samuccaya*, state that it is devoid of the meaning of functional activity (*kāritra*).
The meaning of being produced from causes;
the meaning of being devoid of a sentient being;
the meaning of dependent origination.
The meaning of being immovable;
the meaning of impermanence;
the meaning of abiding for a brief moment.
The meaning of the uninterrupted succession of cause and effect;
the meaning of the similarity between cause and effect;
and the meaning of the diversity of causes and effects.
The meaning of the mutual determination of cause and effect is the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
As for the term "mind," the nature of the conditions of dependent origination is the true realm of the secret heart-treasury of all Buddhas.
This treatise also clarifies this same meaning;
therefore, it speaks of "mind" (*citta*). Furthermore, the term "mind" is also a collective designation.
Because all of these herein encompass extensive meanings,
that which is called "treatise" (śāstra) is so named because it instructs students; thus,
the second statement clarifies what constitutes a correct treatise.
The main gate is divided into two parts:
first, the extensive;
second, the concise.
Regarding the "extensive," it refers to the first five verses among the seven. Regarding the "concise," it refers to the final two verses.
Within the extensive section, it is further divided into five parts.
The "One, Three, and Twelvefold Compendium" refers to the first two verses;
the "Twelve Links of Phenomena Arising Mutually Without Beginning or End" refers to the third verse.
Because the thirty-two factors are empty of self-nature, there is the "Gate of Non-Self," which constitutes the middle verse of the stanza.
Because the forty-two factors are free from the two extremes, there is the "Gate of No Transmigration."
That is, from the verse beginning with "merely following the dharma of emptiness" up to "does not shift," the five gates of cessation (*nirodha*) are as the verse says: "wisdom should examine.
Among those five, the first four are conformable (*anuloma*).
The latter one is a transgression;
this should be reflected upon according to reason.
Between the two approaches—the extensive and the concise—I shall first clarify the extensive one.
Within this extensive [treatise], I shall now first clarify the three categories that subsume the twelve gates.
This section contains two parts;
first, the question.

The subsequent response states that "the prior question" refers to the first half-verse, while "the subsequent answer" refers to the latter one and a half verses; thus the text is correlated accordingly. First, the wording of the question is briefly explained as follows:

"Among these" refers to the introductory statement; that is, within this context of the two teachings—extensive and concise—concerning dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the nature of conditions (*pratyayatā*) as taught by the Tathāgata. As for the term "śramaṇa":
This is the Brahma-voice.
It is translated here as "Well-Trained" and also as "Well-Quiescent."
This refers to the various noble ones (*ārya*) and the community of those who have gone forth following them;
this includes both those within and outside the Buddhist fold. As for the phrase "those who delight in hearing," it is intended to exclude those who lack faith and those who lack interest.
Although there are many desires and cravings, herein one wishes to clearly hear the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
"One who is able to listen" refers to one whose faculty of hearing is unimpaired and who understands the meaning of sounds. "One who is well able to remember and retain" refers to...
This refers to the meaning previously heard by the ear-faculty,

which the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) retains and focuses upon a single object without forgetting. Regarding the term "capable of awakening," it refers to the mental consciousness retaining the meaning that has been understood.
By means of wisdom, one skillfully contemplates the meaning of what is heard;
there is nothing further to be discarded, for all is fully understood.
As for "one who can contemplate," this refers to one who skillfully observes the merits and faults of all phenomena as well as the path to liberation.
Regarding the mention of "possessing discernment and rejection":

because one correctly discriminates among the webs of doubt and remorse concerning the virtues and faults of the defiled and purified categories, these constitute two of the aforementioned five virtues—
namely, the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and [the wisdom derived from reflection].
The first is the virtue of benevolence (*anugraha*);
the latter two are the cultivation of benevolence.
Although it is said that there are five virtues, they also possess the perception of the five kinds of goodness.
One should abandon the five erroneous conceptions and reflect according to the principle.

Regarding the phrase "coming to the place of the teacher," it means that a disciple endowed with the five virtues comes to the place of the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna for the sake of seeking the Dharma. Regarding the phrase "within the teaching of the Tathāgata,"...
A disciple endowed with the five virtues harbors no doubts regarding the teachings of the six external teachers and others;

rather, it is because he has conceived doubts concerning the two meanings of dependent origination—the extensive and the concise—as taught by the Tathāgata that he asks this question. As for the term "Bhagavān": [it refers to the Blessed One].
This is called "subduing.
It means being fully endowed with the subduing of the four māras and possessing the six qualities. Question:
As for the term Bhagavat, what does it signify?
Only the Tathāgata has attained it.
For what reason is the Teacher called Bhagavat? Answer:
Because his disciples conceive the notion of the Tathāgata toward their Teacher.

Words of Reverence: Furthermore, this Nāgārjuna, abiding in the stage of the Path of Vision (darśanamārga), abandoned all unwholesome dharmas and remained far removed from the realm of Māra; as it is stated in the sūtras with truthful words:
"All dharmas are like an illusion."
He speaks for the sake of all sentient beings,
and therein he is fearless;
therefore, he is called Bhagavat.
The Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna realized the Stage of Supreme Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) and understood that all phenomena arising through dependent origination are like illusions and transformations.
Because he possesses such virtues, his words do not contradict the ultimate truth. As for the disciples addressing their teacher as "Bhagavān": [this is done out of respect].
"What do you seek? It is for the sake of the exhaustion of craving;
it is for the sake of liberation."
It is not for the sake of material gain or the fruits of affection. As for what they are subsumed under:
it is because those disciples have already understood the broad meaning beforehand.
Because [the interlocutor] is unskilled in the method of summary, he asks about the meaning of that summary.

The phrase "now desiring to hear" implies that although one says "desiring to hear," it also includes reflection (*cintā*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā*) for the sake of attaining the fruit. Next, the words of the response are explained:

To know that he asked about its true meaning means that the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna knew that those disciples endowed with the five virtues [inquired] regarding the nature of dependent origination, both in its full extent (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and in its mode of being (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
In the midst of the true meaning, there is no way that the arising of yearning and reverence is not in accordance with the Dharma;
therefore, I ask this question tentatively. As for the Master’s addressing [the disciple] as "you," it is because that disciple has previously formed the perception of the Teacher as the Tathāgata.
To address the Bhagavat as being endowed with those qualities is to call him "Thou. Regarding the term "Teacher" (ācārya), it refers to the five types of teachers:
the teacher of ordination (*pravrajyā-karmācārya*), the teacher of dependence (*niśrayācārya*), and the teacher of instruction (*śikṣācārya*). Regarding the term "Thou": [it is used here].
This refers to "sons.
There are three kinds of sons:
first, those born from one's own body.
The second arises from speech;
the third arises from the mind.
Now, we take the latter two. To say "making this clear" means:
Furthermore, because the words and their meanings do not contradict one another, they accord with the questions and answers;
thus, the speech is clear and distinct. Regarding the phrase "words of canonical efficacy," it means that the speech is free from error and devoid of confusion.
The principles are clearly elucidated so that the audience may obtain beneficial results.

Next, the following section again provides a detailed explanation of the questions raised in the treatise. Regarding the statement, "Because there are ten and two herein, they are called twelve": this means...
If the ten and the two were not stated separately, the number would be twenty;
this statement is made because there would be the fault of redundancy. Question:
Why does it not say "eleven"?
It does not say thirteen;
it definitively says twelve.
What is meant by this?
If one says that eleven meanings are insufficient, or that thirteen meanings are useless, there would be the fault of addition or subtraction;
therefore, they are fixed at twelve. Furthermore, because the causal functioning of the three periods of time requires twelve factors.
That is to say, from the prior limit to the middle limit, the causes are ignorance, volitional formations, and consciousness;
the result is name-and-form;
and the auxiliary cause is craving.
From the middle point to the subsequent end, the causes range from consciousness to sensation;
the results are birth, old age, and death;
and the auxiliary causes are grasping and becoming.
Those abiding in the middle period range from consciousness to feeling;
therefore, there are definitely twelve. Furthermore, regarding these twelve, the first three are the projecting factors (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*).
Name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are the factors that are projected.
Craving, grasping, and becoming are the factors that bring about actualization.
Birth is the single factor that constitutes the result.
Old age and death are the factors of affliction (*ādīnava-aṅga*).
As for the projecting factors (*ākṣepaka-aṅga*),
they reveal the remote causes.
That which is capable of accomplishing [the result] indicates the proximate cause;

for if these two were absent, birth would not be established. It is called a "limb" (aṅga) because it is a specific differentiation; just as one speaks of the "limbs" of a chariot because they are its constituent parts, so too are these called limbs.
Apart from the twelve links, there is no separate distinction;
rather, because the nature, characteristics, functions, and names of these twelve links differ, they are established as distinct entities, just like the various parts of a chariot.
If there is no chariot apart from its wheels and other parts,
this case is likewise so.
This is the clarification of the nature and characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination.
As stated in the *Śālistamba-sūtra*:

"What is ignorance? It is the arising, with respect to these six elements, of the notion of unity, the notion of a whole, the notion of permanence, the notion of solidity, the notion of indestructibility, the notion of happiness, and the notions of 'sentient being,' 'living being,' 'nourisher,' 'person,' 'individual,' 'youth,' 'agent,' 'self,' and 'mine.'"
And other various forms of non-knowing—
this is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because of the presence of ignorance, one gives rise to greed, hatred, and delusion toward all objects.
That which gives rise to greed, hatred, and delusion toward various objects is "conditioned by ignorance,
there are volitional formations" (*avidyā-pratyayāḥ saṃskārāḥ*);
whereas that which is able to discern among those various phenomena is [consciousness].
That which is called "consciousness," together with the four aggregates of clinging that arise simultaneously with consciousness—
this is name-and-form (nāmarūpa).
The various faculties based upon name-and-form are called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The conjunction of these three factors is termed contact (*sparśa*).
The experiencing of contact is called feeling (vedanā);
one becomes attached to that feeling.
This is called craving.
That which increases craving is called grasping.
That which arises from grasping and is capable of producing karma is called "existence" (bhava).
The aggregates produced from those causes are called "birth.
Once born, the maturation of the aggregates is [called aging].
This is called aging.
When the aggregates have already perished and disintegrated,
this is called death.
At the time of death, that which is internally possessed of attachment and feverish distress is called sorrow (*śoka*);
from this sorrow arise various words and expressions.

The consciousness that attends to mental objects and experiences various forms of suffering is called sorrow (*daurmanasya*).
One who possesses these and the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) [is so described].
It is called "affliction. Regarding the clarification of the functional activity of the twelve links of dependent origination, as stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:
"What is the function of ignorance?"
Furthermore, it serves as a condition for sentient beings who are deluded regarding the various realms of existence (*bhava*) and for the formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
What function do the formative forces perform so that sentient beings appear within the various destinies?
It also serves as the condition for the arising of the habitual tendencies of consciousness.
What function does consciousness perform that enables it to maintain the entanglements of sentient beings' karma?
It also acts as the condition for name-and-form.
What function does name-and-form perform such that it causes sentient beings to take up a body and also acts as a condition for the six sense bases?
What function do the six sense bases perform such that they cause sentient beings to fully acquire a body and act as a condition for contact?
What is the function of contact? It causes sentient beings to experience objects by serving as the condition for feeling.
What is the function of feeling? It causes sentient beings to seek rebirth by serving as the condition for craving.
What function does craving perform such that it serves as the condition for grasping, which in turn leads sentient beings toward birth?
What function does grasping perform such that, by way of taking up future existence (*punarbhava*), it serves as the condition for the consciousness of sentient beings that possesses grasping?
What kind of karma acts as the condition that causes sentient beings to proceed toward future existence?
What kind of karma acts so as to cause the successive formation of name-and-form and the six sense bases for sentient beings?
Furthermore, contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are the conditions for old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

What function does old age and death perform such that it causes sentient beings to repeatedly undergo transformation of their lifespan and life-force? Regarding the explanation of the names of the twelve factors (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma*): [text continues].
As stated in the *Śālistamba-sūtra*:
"Because it is a great darkness, it is called ignorance (*avidyā*);
because it performs formative activity, it is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)."
It is called "consciousness" (vijñāna) because it discerns;
it is called "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) because they are mutually dependent;
it is called the "six sense bases" (ṣaḍāyatana) because they serve as gateways for arising.
Contact is called "contact" because it contacts;
feeling is called "feeling" because it feels;
craving is called "craving" because it thirsts.
It is called "clinging" (upādāna) because it grasps;
it is called "existence" (bhava) because it produces future existence;
it is called "birth" (jāti) because it gives rise to the aggregates.
The maturation of the aggregates is called aging;
the disintegration of the aggregates is called death;
and grief is called sorrow.
It is called "sighing" (daurmanasya) because it involves lamentation; it is called "suffering" (duḥkha) because it afflicts the body;
and it is called "grief" (śoka) because it afflicts the mind.
It is called "affliction" (nigha) because it afflicts; it is called "Able One" (Śākyamuni) because he can pacify body and speech.
Although it is not explicitly stated that the mind can pacify body and speech, [the pacification] arises from the cause of the purity of that very mind.
It is simply that the purity of the fruit is known;
it is not mentioned because of the purity of the cause.
To say that it is not of intrinsic nature [means]:
Below that are ten kinds [of views].
This is the first [category], the heterodox and deviant attachments of non-Buddhists.
Specifically, the naked ascetics (nirgranthas) cling to six types of phenomena as being the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena.
First, those with life;
second, those without life;
third, those with outflows.
Fourth, the acquisition of fetters;
fifth, the observance of precepts;
sixth, liberation.
If one does not discern these six phenomena, one wanders in saṃsāra;
if one discerns them, one attains liberation.
There may be a certain class of people who cling to the notion that [these phenomena] exist.
The subtle, minute, and obscure darkness of passion is the equal self-nature;
that very person is the self-nature of the Dharma.
Regarding the two words "definitive":
This is the tenet of the Sāṃkhya outsiders.
They maintain that there is a certain category [of cause] such that whatever arises from it is its effect.
That itself is the cause.
Therefore, the causes and effects are each determined for the various realms such as humans and devas;
they do not dwell in confusion, but revolve through the cycle of birth and death.
The third term, "person" (puruṣa),
also belongs to the Sāṃkhya school;
it refers to a certain class who cling to the notion that [the self] exists.
Sentient beings and the person (*pudgala*) are the causes of all phenomena.
Failing to understand these two, they dwell for a long time in birth and death;
yet though they abide in mutual confusion, when they achieve clear discernment, they immediately attain liberation.
A person who possesses a thousand verses of skillful exposition on the Dharma,
or one who maintains that a person has great power and efficacy.
Each dwells within the body of sentient beings.
Regarding the fourth point, "mutual dependence," it refers to a certain class of non-Buddhists who say:
The days, months, and constellations are the causes of the Dharma;

If one contravenes them, it will not be accomplished.

If there are sentient beings who bathe their limbs in the Ganges River and other such waters,

There is a certain class of people who cling to the notion that purification is achieved through solitude and the like;
they hold that karmic maturation is accomplished without depending on good or evil,
but rather that purity is attained merely through methods such as bathing in the sun and moon.
Regarding the "Masters of the Five Verses":
this is also a school of the Sāṃkhya doctrine.
It refers to a certain group who assert as follows:
The suffering and pleasure experienced by sentient beings do not arise from good and evil;
although they transform them with apparent autonomy,

Why is this? It is because we observe that in this world, when sentient beings wish to cultivate pure karma during the causal stage,
they do not achieve their original intention.
On the contrary, it becomes even more evil;

"The six [factors] are called 'time'."

The phrase "equally encompassing all other heterodox attachments" does not refer solely to what precedes;
the term "arising from the ten words" is to be applied individually to each of the nine preceding passages.
Regarding the statement that "these are produced by causes and conditions":
among the internal and external phenomena taught by the Muni, the nature of dependent origination consists solely of primary causes and auxiliary causes.

Because there is no other self-nature and because they are determined [as such], the following section—the second part of the first gate—clarifies the response and explains the treatise. Regarding the statement: "These twelve distinct factors of existence, which mutually depend upon one another like bundles of reeds within the categories of afflictions, karma, and suffering, are all fully subsumed within those three": [This means that] these twelve links of dependent origination rely on each other through the cycle of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma (*karman*), and suffering (*duḥkha*), just as the stalks of a bundle of reeds lean against one another; thus, all [phenomena] are entirely contained within these three.
For example, in the world, a house is constructed using bundles of reeds and other materials; it cannot be established by a single component alone.

In this same way, the twelve links of dependent origination are fully subsumed within three categories; through their conjunction and mutual dependence, they collectively produce the causes and effects of both the defiled and purified classes of phenomena, such that no single factor possesses supremacy on its own.
"If even one [member] were omitted, it would not be complete; the term 'exhaustive' (kṛtsna) means 'without remainder' (niravaśeṣa).

This means that among these three categories of phenomena, there is not a single factor among the twelve links of dependent origination that is not subsumed; thus, the causes and effects of affliction (saṃkleśa) are exhaustively and universally encompassed.
Therefore, because the doubts questioned by the disciples of the five virtues have all been severed.

Furthermore, the subsequent phrase "it was asked" (*wen yue*) and so forth is the introductory text for the following response. As for the phrase "it was asked": (Note: This is a commentary on a Buddhist scripture, explaining that the initial question posed by the disciples serves as the catalyst for the Master’s subsequent answer.)
The Disciple of Five Virtues Questions the Teacher: He asks, "What is affliction?
What is karma? What is the vision of suffering?"
Regarding these distinct dharmas, by what should they be subsumed as a guiding principle?
The Master said:
"By which three dharmas are the twelve subsumed?"
The explicit discourse on the functions of the scriptures has already been clearly explained, and I have understood its distinctions.

Among the twelve factors (*dvādaśa-dharma*), how many are comprised within the path of afflictions (*kleśa-mārga*), how many are the path of karma (*karma-mārga*), and how many are the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*)? How many are causes (*hetu*) and how many are results (*phala*)?
"I now have doubts and request an explanation; therefore, I have raised this question.
As for the phrase "the answer is given," it refers to the teacher responding in order to sever the disciple's doubts.
Regarding the statement that the first, eighth, and ninth [categories] are afflictions:

it is because these three factors disturb sentient beings in a manner identical to the nature of afflictions; therefore, they are subsumed under "afflictions" on account of their functional similarity, not because their essential natures are identical.
That is to say: because ignorance disturbs the mind when one is not clearly aware of an object;
because craving disturbs the mind when one is attached to an object;
and because grasping disturbs the mind when one is intensely engaged in the practice of pursuing an object.
The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* states: "The three paths—

the path of affliction consisting of ignorance, craving, and grasping, which are distinct yet intermingled with suffering and its origin— and the two paths of volitional formations and existence, proceed without interruption."
The path of action consisting of mental factors (*dharmakarmapatha*) does not sever the remaining seven branches;

likewise, the path of suffering consisting of mental factors does not sever them. This treatise and the meaning of the Sūtra are identical on this point. As for the statement regarding "two and ten paths of action consisting of views": [the two] refer to the view of self-existence (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); [the ten] refer to the remaining eight views plus wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and the view of holding to views as supreme (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).

Because these two factors, though differing in their essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), are identical in their sense of volitional activity (*abhisamskāra*), they are designated by the term "karma" (*karman*).

That is to say, the *saṃskāras* perform karma—such as merit (*puṇya*)—by means of the doors of body, speech, and mind, thereby producing further existence (*punarbhava*). As for the statement that "the remaining seven are all suffering":

Because these seven factors all arise from the defilement of karma and share the same characteristic of result, and because they possess the nature of the threefold suffering, they are designated by the name "suffering. In the sūtras and various treatises, ignorance is listed first and old age and death last.
What is the underlying meaning for the sequence being thus?
It is because sentient beings, from time immemorial, have failed to understand cause and effect as well as true nature, and thus remain in delusion.
From delusion there arises volitional formation.
Through the habitual tendencies of formations, the mind becomes inverted;
because the mind is inverted, one continues to take birth in the future.
Due to the continuity of name-and-form (nāmarūpa), the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana) are established.
Because the sense faculties are established, there is contact with objects;
through that contact, one experiences the enjoyment of those objects.
Because one experiences objects, one becomes attached to them in the present and gives rise to craving for the future.
Because craving arises, there is grasping and accumulation.
Because of this accumulation, the existence that serves as the cause for rebirth is accomplished.
Because there is arising, one undergoes birth within the five destinies.
Because there is birth, there is aging and death.
Thus, all classes of sentient beings have transmigrated through birth and death since beginningless time.
This is because the sequence of cause and effect is thus.
The sequence being such,
the phenomena of ignorance and so forth each exist as distinct and individual entities.
Within each and every dharma there are distinctions;
namely, ignorance consists of nineteen types.
The first is ignorance regarding the prior limit (*pūrvānta*).
2. Ignorance regarding the future;
3. Ignorance regarding both [the past and the future];
4. Ignorance regarding the internal.
5. Lack of knowledge regarding external objects;
6. Lack of knowledge regarding both internal and external objects;
7. Lack of knowledge regarding karma.
8. Ignorance regarding maturation;
9. Ignorance regarding the maturation of karma;
10. Ignorance regarding the Buddha.
Eleventh, ignorance regarding the Dharma;
twelfth, ignorance regarding the Saṅgha;
thirteenth, ignorance regarding suffering.
14. Ignorance regarding the origin;
15. Ignorance regarding cessation;
16. Ignorance regarding the path.
Seventeenth, ignorance regarding causes;
eighteenth, ignorance regarding effects;
nineteenth, ignorance regarding the bases.
There are three kinds of formations:
namely, unwholesome formations, meritorious formations, and immovable formations.
There are eight kinds of consciousness.
This refers to everything from visual consciousness up to the ālayavijñāna.
Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is twofold:
first, the complete [name-and-form].
This refers to the two lower realms,
which lack completeness;
that is to say, the formless realm.
There are six bases of cognition (ṣaḍāyatana),
namely the eye-faculty and so forth;
and there are six types of contact (sparśa).
This refers to everything from eye-contact to mind-contact.
There are eighteen types of feeling,
meaning that each of the six faculties— from the eye to the mind— is endowed with three types of feeling.
There are three kinds of grasping (upādāna),
namely craving for the three realms.
There are four kinds of clinging (upādāna).
This refers to the desire to see [the truth regarding] prohibitions and the doctrine of the self.
There are twelve [categories], namely:
birth, fruit, karma, accumulation, death, birth, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), the three realms, and the five destinies (*gati*).
There are four modes of birth, namely, birth from a womb and so forth. The distinctions of old age consist of such things as white hair and wrinkled faces.

The distinctions of death consist of such things as the cessation of life, the exhaustion of the life-faculty, and the dissolution of the vital force. The phrase "all these" serves as a comprehensive summary.
It is said that the teachings of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna speak of eight types of suffering and seven dharmas, such as consciousness;
however, they only subsume five of them and do not mention the remaining three. Why is this so?
To refute this objection, the word "all" is used to include the three types of suffering.
As for how the seven factors, beginning with consciousness, encompass the five [aggregates]:
it is said that consciousness, name-and-form, and the six sense bases encompass the suffering of the five aggregates in their state of full development (*bhava-duḥkha*).
The two phenomena of sensation (*vedanā*) and contact (*sparśa*) include the suffering of illness;
birth includes the suffering of birth;
and old age and death include the suffering of aging and the suffering of death. Furthermore, a sutra says:
Regarding the three types of suffering and the eight types of suffering:
these merely subsume the eight within the three.
Furthermore, how is it that consciousness and name-and-form are identified as the six modes of suffering?
The two factors of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are themselves the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*).

Birth and old age and death are the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). Therefore, it is said that these twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) are situated within karma and the afflictions (*kleśa*).
This refers to the words of the *Vyākhyāyukti* (Explanatory Commentary) which state that the twelve [bases] are subsumed within the three [categories] as expressed in the verse.
The word "only" (*kevala*) has the sense of exclusion;
it refers to the dharmas taught in the Sūtra.
The phrase "this includes everything exhaustively,
with nothing remaining" demonstrates the superior efficacy of the treatise.
This treatise is inconceivable because it universally encompasses the vast meaning of all sūtras.

Next follows the second major section of the commentary, which clarifies the gate wherein the twelve links of dependent origination arise from one another in succession, having neither beginning nor end. Regarding the question: "This meaning is already known; however, how do those afflictions, karma, and suffering arise in succession? Please provide an explanation."
Regarding the inclusion of the twelve links of dependent origination within the three paths,
the Master composed clear and authoritative words concerning them;
therein lies both the nature of all that exists (*yāvadbhāvikatā*) and the nature of things as they are (*yathāvadbhāvikatā*).
I now understand all those twelve factors without error:
what is the cause, and what is the fruit?
How do they arise in mutual succession?
Regarding all causes and effects, we now desire to hear them; please explain this for us.

This reveals one's own capacity as well as the process of origination. To say that "the two types of karma arise from the three afflictions" means that volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) arise from ignorance (*avidyā*), and existence (*bhava*) arises from craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*).
To say "referring to the dharmas of suffering mentioned above" [is as follows].

This refers to what is stated in the preceding section on the "Gate of the Anterior": that consciousness gives rise to name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death;
that is to say, from volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) through consciousness (*vijñāna*) up to feeling (*vedanā*), these five factors arise.
Because birth arises from existence, there are birth, old age, and death.
What are called the various afflictions are precisely ignorance, craving, and grasping.
That is to say, from consciousness through sensation, craving and grasping arise;
and from birth and old age and death, ignorance arises.
Thus, the twelve factors of existence are produced one from another in mutual succession.
Among the four conditions, how many conditions does each possess as its conditioning factors?
Each excludes the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya) and possesses the remaining three conditions.
If ignorance gives rise to bodily and vocal formations that are material in nature, [it acts as a condition through the remaining three].
It acts as a condition by way of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
If it gives rise to mental formations that are non-material,
it acts as a condition by way of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
In this way, as for the remaining factors: if they produce that which is material, they act as conditions by way of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*);

if they produce that which is non-material, they act as conditions by way of the object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition.
In this way, that which is non-material serves as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for that which is material;
furthermore, it also serves as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), an object condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and a dominant condition for that which is non-material.
It should be understood that why do the twelve factors of dependent origination not serve as one another’s *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition)?
This is because the *hetu-pratyaya* manifests from each factor's own respective seed.
There is further extensive textual material on this broad meaning, which is not described here for fear of prolixity.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: "Regarding 'existence,' there are three kinds, namely: desire, form, and formlessness."
This demonstrates the existence of the three realms.
The desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is so called because one has not yet abandoned the craving for desires; it is named the desire realm.
The form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is so called because one has already abandoned the craving for desires but has not yet abandoned the craving for form; it is named the form realm.

The formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) refers to those who have already abandoned desire for sensual pleasures and abandoned desire for the form realm, yet have not yet abandoned desire for the formless realm;
this is called the formless realm. As for the beings of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are ten kinds.
First, the existence of the desire realm (kāmadhātu-bhava) existing from beginningless time;
second, karmic existence (karma-bhava);
and third, death-existence (maraṇa-bhava).
Fourth, the intermediate existence;
fifth, the existence at birth;
sixth, the existence in the hells.
7. Existence among animals;
8. Existence in the realm of hungry ghosts;
9. Existence in the human realm.
The ten destinies constitute existence; this is called "existence in the desire realm" (*kāmadhātu-bhava*).
Among these, the first, third, and fifth are termed "existence by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-bhava*).
The proponent fully cites the meaning of its result to establish the sense of "existence" (*bhava*).
As for the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is called "existence" because it attains the sense of a subsequent existence (*punarbhava*) as its result.
As for the five destinies (*pañcagati*), they are called "existence" because they possess the sense of experiencing [the results] as their fruit.
The existence of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-bhava*) consists of the remaining six destinies, excluding the three evil paths and the human realm.
The existence of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu-bhava*) consists of the remaining five fruits, excluding the three evil paths, the human realm, and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Regarding the statement that it revolves incessantly within this:
it means that within the three realms of existence, there is no moment of abiding, and it has neither beginning nor end,
due to the predominant power of the causes of afflictions and karma.

Because they experience the fruits of suffering within the three realms and five destinies, the metaphor of the wheel is employed to illustrate the meaning of non-abiding. It is said that those various ordinary beings wander through the world of their own accord.
This means that within the three realms of existence, there is no cessation;
although the wheel of saṃsāra revolves, there is no agent,
but only diverse causes and diverse effects.
Because they wander aimlessly without any benefit or purpose, the repetition of the word "this" indicates the sense of indeterminacy;
it is not like the sequential arising of various existences through cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
This refers to the indeterminate [state].
It is because sentient beings are born into the three realms and five destinies according to their karma,
without any fixed sequence.
Next, the third major section below explains the gate of the selflessness of phenomena through the emptiness of the twelve links [of dependent origination]. The commentary asks:
"What is it that constitutes a sentient being who possesses mastery over this body?"
What is the nature of its activity?
This is the question raised at the beginning of the treatise.
This refers to the Master’s prior teaching on the three categories that subsume the twelve links and their mutual relationship of arising.
He stated that there are only these twelve and nothing else.
If this were so, then every sentient being within the various realms of existence would possess autonomy within their own bodies, and thus they would all be called "sentient beings" (sattva).
Yet, one immediately gives rise to the notion of a "sentient being" regarding that [entity].
Why do you not explain what it is that the multitude collectively refers to as its "original non-existence"?
If such a thing exists, what are its characteristics, nature, and functional activities?
I pray that the Master will explain this.

To speak of "mastery" refers to seeing, hearing, and so forth. To say that the various realms of existence consist solely of cause and effect, excluding only conventional designations, and that therein there are no sentient beings—[this is what is meant].
That which refers to the three realms, the four modes of birth, and the five destinies is called "the various destinies.
These very destinies arise solely from the causes of afflictions and karma as their resultant suffering;
it is upon this cause and effect that the designation "sentient beings" is conventionally established.
Based on those [factors], one conventionally designates the notion of a "sentient being";
for apart from those causes and effects, there is no other sentient being whatsoever.
This is because the treatise is concise.
Although it is said that there are no sentient beings, this also includes the various erroneous designations such as *pudgala*, *puruṣa*, *kāraka*, and so forth;
therefore, the Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra and other treatises state:
The meaning of being devoid of a sentient being is the meaning of dependent origination.
Within being devoid of a sentient being, there is further the meaning of impermanence.
If it is impermanent, it further has the meaning of momentary abiding.
If it were to abide even momentarily, it would be dependent upon another;
if it is dependent upon another, it is devoid of the meaning of agency.
This is the meaning of dependent origination, as explained at length in the treatise. To say "this is the ultimate meaning, not a conventionally established existence" means:
This refers to the profound meaning of the nature of dependent origination regarding the absence of sentient beings and so forth;
whether Buddhas appear in the world or do not appear, their fundamental nature remains thus.
This is not like the false conceptualizations of the non-Buddhists;
because we provisionally establish that it also exists,
it is called "real."
Regarding the statement that the object of conventional designation is not an established real entity,
there is an objection: "If that conventionally designated sentient being exists,
then the conventionally designated sentient being is indeed existent."
Therefore, for what reason do you say that there are no sentient beings herein?
This statement was made to answer this objection.
Hereafter begins the fourth major section of the commentary, which clarifies that the twelve links of existence are free from the two extremes and thus do not undergo transmigration.
This section on the refutation is divided into two parts:
first, the principle;
second, the analogy.
This is the analysis of the division. The discourse says:
"If it is thus—namely, that in the aforementioned realms of existence there are only causes and effects and no sentient beings therein—it is because it is so.
As for the question, 'Who goes from this world to another world?'"
If there were no self, person, sentient being, or life-span,
who would transmigrate from this world to another world to undergo the retribution for good and evil karma?
Furthermore, if there were no self that goes to another world, [how could this be?]
The non-Buddhists also claim that there is no other world and establish the doctrine of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).

What is the distinction between these? The answer states: "There are no such things as atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth" means that within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), not even the slightest thing reaches another world. As for the phrase "nevertheless": [it refers to the following].

Although not even the slightest dharma among the five aggregates passes over to another world, it is solely because from empty dharmas there arises again an empty dharma that this occurs. As for the statement, "solely from empty dharmas there arises again an empty dharma":
The meaning of this verse is to clarify that because dharmas such as atoms do not exist within the cause, they arise through transformation when reaching the fruit.
As the Sūtra says:
"Karma, once performed, perishes."
Once extinguished, they do not abide in any location;
nevertheless, at the time of death, each appears within the mind as if dwelling nearby.
Thus it is, Great King, when the final consciousness ceases.
The consciousness of the birth-process first arises in the realms of humans, devas, and so forth.
Not a single dharma migrates from this world to another world;
nevertheless, there is the apparent relinquishing of the life-span and the arising of the initial state of birth.
The final cessation of consciousness is called the relinquishing of life;
the initial arising of consciousness is called the phenomenon of birth.
That which ceases at the end has no destination to which it goes.
Phenomena that arise for the first time come from nowhere.
Why is this? Because their intrinsic nature is quiescent.
Subsequently, consciousness and emptiness relinquish the life-force;
the life-force is relinquished by emptiness and karma;
and karma itself is empty.
Initial consciousness is the emptiness of the initial [moment]; that which arises is the emptiness of arising.
Nevertheless, karma is not lost.
Therefore, this treatise accords with the meaning of the sūtras.
Other commentaries and their terminology are self-evident and need not be discussed further.
Next, below, the analogy will be explained. Regarding the phrase "herein it is asked," etc., these are words of request.
"From emptiness, emptiness arises.
Because it is subtle and difficult to comprehend, an analogy is requested.
As for the statement that this response establishes eight analogies and so forth: [this refers to the following].
Although they expound a single meaning, many metaphors are established because the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings are unequal.
As for the "aggregates of speech," these are the aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The full extent of the characteristics of these five aggregates is as explained in other treatises, such as the *Pañcaskandhaka*. Here,
their characteristics will be briefly analyzed.
Regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*):
it refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the various forms derived from the four great elements. Regarding the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*):
it refers to the three types of experience.
First, suffering;
second, pleasure;
third, neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Pleasure is defined as the desire for union that exists at the time of cessation;
suffering is defined as the desire for separation that exists at the time of arising;
neither-suffering-nor-pleasure is defined as the absence of both desires.
Regarding the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*):
it refers to the grasping of various signs (*nimitta*) with respect to objects.
This, moreover, is threefold.
This refers to limited perception (*parīttasaṃjñā*), vast perception (*mahadgata-saṃjñā*), and immeasurable perception (*apramāṇa-saṃjñā*). Regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*):

it refers to all other mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) apart from feeling and perception, as well as the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*). Regarding the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*): [it refers to...]
It has the nature of discerning its respective objects.
This, moreover, is threefold:
first, the six evolving consciousnesses.
The second is the manas-vijñāna;
the third is the ālaya-vijñāna. As for "continuous connection," it refers to that which arises from those causes after [the preceding state] has ceased.
If cause and effect were distinct and not intermingled, such that the cause perishes and the effect arises,
they would be like the rise and fall of the ends of a balance scale— occurring in the same single moment without any temporal interval. Therefore,
it is said that there is "cyclic flow."
Subsequently, the ten dharmas flow and revolve due to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of false conceptualization within emptiness;
these are precisely the habitual tendencies of false conceptualization that constitute the bitter fruit of the ten dharmas.
They are the five causal dharmas of afflictions and karma.
Next follows the fifth major section, which clarifies the gate of cessation and return (*nivṛtti*). Regarding the terms "subsequent" and "should," these constitute a reverse contemplation;
one should understand that their meaning is the opposite [of the preceding].
Regarding those who provide commentaries on the words [of the sūtras],
they should be examined for consistency with the wisdom of the verses of the aforementioned treatise;
hence the subsequent use of the term "should."
One should know that this is the reverse of those three paths of the causes and effects of affliction (*saṃkleśa*). Herein there is a question:
"In what way is it the reverse of those three paths of the causes and effects of affliction?"
It is for the purpose of revealing the true path of the noble ones that it is said:
"One should contemplate all phenomena as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. Regarding the phrase "one should contemplate all phenomena":
This refers to contemplating the twelve factors as a flowing stream of light.

That which is called "impermanent" is because phenomena such as ignorance have the nature of disintegration and destruction. That which is called "suffering" is because phenomena such as ignorance have the nature of suffering [as indicated by the missing characters].
That which is called "emptiness" is ignorance.
